items.title: Microchip earnings beat contrasts with supply-constrained guidance and steep share decline
items.summary: Microchip Technology reported strong September-quarter growth and adjusted earnings above guidance, but its shares fell sharply as the December outlook pointed to a sequential revenue decline. Lengthening manufacturing lead times, capacity limitations and delayed high-margin orders complicate near-term margins despite underlying industrial and data-center demand. These are observed market and operating signals, not proof of a lasting impairment.

items.title: Marvell and Lumentum face extraordinary weekly losses after all-stock AI connectivity merger
items.summary: Shares of both companies suffered exceptionally large weekly declines despite a Friday rebound, as investors reassessed Marvell's proposed acquisition of Lumentum. The announced $1,132 valuation is based on pre-announcement prices, not fixed cash consideration: each Lumentum share would receive 4.5 Marvell shares. Strong optical and semiconductor demand remains possible, while exchange-ratio exposure, regulatory approval and integration complicate valuation.

items.title: Iran-linked vessel anomalies near Gulf of Oman subsea cables add digital-infrastructure risk
items.summary: Windward's October 29 assessment documented three sanctioned tankers and an Iran-flagged fishing-support vessel making unusual movements near subsea cable corridors during October 5–28. Financial Times coverage renewed attention on November 6. Tracking anomalies are a leading security signal, not evidence that any cable was attacked or that mine placement occurred.

items.title: Microsoft reportedly winds down rented Oracle AI computing as hardware becomes less suitable
items.summary: Bloomberg, cited by Reuters, reports Microsoft has been switching off rented Oracle AI computing after declining to renew an older arrangement. The Nvidia hardware reportedly no longer meets Microsoft's evolving needs. This raises utilization and asset-obsolescence questions for AI infrastructure providers, but Microsoft has not directly confirmed the reported nonrenewal.

items.title: JMIC shipping assessment documents persistent Hormuz traffic disruption
items.summary: The November 5 JMIC assessment reports attacks and persistently depressed commercial vessel movements through Hormuz relative to the 2025 baseline. US-assisted passages continued but fell slightly from the prior reporting period. These measurements establish ongoing maritime stress, not a new oil-volume loss caused by Friday's reported tanker incident.

observations.value: 4 across reporting period; 3 in previous period; incidents November 1-3

observations.label: Overall commercial transit vs historical baseline
observations.value: Substantially below 2025 levels; independent tracking showed single-digit to low-double-digit movements per day

observations.label: US-assisted vessel transits, current reporting period
observations.value: Approximately 31 per day, versus 34 per day during October 24-30; not equivalent to overall traffic

observations.label: Additional petroleum throughput lost on November 6
observations.value: Not independently established

items.key_finding: JMIC data support ongoing severe Hormuz shipping stress, without demonstrating a new Friday petroleum-flow shock.
